CORE CURRICULUM

Strategies worth trading

Each approach below covers what it is, when it works, and where traders usually get it wrong.

Structural

Support & Resistance Mapping

Every pair leaves a memory of prices where it has previously reversed or stalled. Support is where buyers have historically stepped in; resistance is where sellers have capped the advance. Traders mark these zones on the daily and 4-hour chart, then watch for reaction — a wick rejection, a stall in momentum, or a clean break with volume — before entering.

Timeframe: 4H – DailyBest in: Ranging marketsRisk note: Zones, not exact lines
Momentum

Breakout Trading

When price compresses inside a tight range — often shown as a triangle or rectangle on the chart — it is storing energy. A breakout strategy waits for a decisive close beyond that range, ideally backed by a rise in volume, and enters in the direction of the break with a stop placed back inside the old range.

Timeframe: 1H – 4HBest in: Pre-news, pre-session movesRisk note: Watch for false breaks
Retracement

Fibonacci Retracement

After a strong impulse move, price rarely travels in a straight line — it pulls back before continuing. The 38.2%, 50%, and 61.8% retracement levels mark the zones where that pullback commonly ends. Traders combine these levels with a support/resistance zone or a candlestick reversal signal to time entries in the direction of the original trend.

Timeframe: 1H – DailyBest in: Trending marketsRisk note: Never used alone
Trend-following

Moving Average Crossover

A fast moving average (such as the 9 or 20 EMA) crossing above a slower one (such as the 50 or 200 EMA) signals a potential shift in trend direction. This strategy is simple to automate and works best on pairs that trend for extended periods, but it lags in choppy, sideways conditions.

Timeframe: 4H – DailyBest in: Strong trendsRisk note: Lags in sideways markets
Price action

Candlestick Reversal Patterns

Patterns like the pin bar, engulfing candle, and doji reveal a shift in the tug-of-war between buyers and sellers at a specific price. Read at a key support or resistance zone, a single well-formed reversal candle can offer a tighter, higher-probability entry than waiting for a full trend change to confirm.

Timeframe: 15M – 4HBest in: Key levelsRisk note: Confirm with the next candle
High frequency

Scalping

Scalping targets small, frequent moves — often just 5 to 15 pips per trade — using the 1-minute or 5-minute chart. It demands tight spreads, fast execution, and strict discipline, since a handful of undisciplined trades can erase an entire session's gains. Best suited to liquid pairs during the London and New York overlap.

Timeframe: 1M – 5MBest in: High liquidity sessionsRisk note: Spread-sensitive
Positional

Swing Trading

Rather than watching every candle, swing traders hold positions for several days to a few weeks, aiming to capture one full leg of a trend. Entries are typically built on a mix of structure, a retracement level, and a higher-timeframe trend filter, which reduces the noise of intraday volatility.

Timeframe: Daily – WeeklyBest in: Clear directional trendsRisk note: Needs wider stops
CHART PATTERN LIBRARY

15 patterns every trader should recognise

Every pattern below marks a typical entry, stop, and target — read them as a starting framework, not a guarantee.

Reversal Patterns Signal a trend is likely to turn
Reversal · Bearish

1. Double Top

Two peaks form at nearly the same level with a pullback (the neckline) between them. A close below the neckline signals the uptrend is exhausted. Entry sits on the neckline break, stop above the peaks, target measured from neckline to peak height.

Reversal · Bearish

2. Head and Shoulders

Three peaks form, with the middle one (the head) higher than the two shoulders. A break of the neckline confirms the reversal. Stop goes above the right shoulder, target is the distance from head to neckline projected downward.

Reversal · Bearish

3. Rising Wedge

Price grinds higher inside two converging, upward-sloping trendlines after an extended advance. Momentum fades as the wedge tightens, and a break below the lower line signals the reversal. Stop above the wedge, target equal to its widest height.

Reversal · Bullish

4. Double Bottom

The mirror image of the double top — two troughs at a similar level with a neckline of resistance between them. A close above the neckline confirms buyers have taken control. Stop below the troughs, target from neckline to trough depth.

Reversal · Bullish

5. Inverse Head and Shoulders

Three troughs form with the middle one lower than the two shoulders either side. Breaking above the neckline confirms a bottom is in. Stop below the right shoulder, target is the head-to-neckline distance projected upward.

Reversal · Bullish

6. Falling Wedge

Two converging, downward-sloping trendlines contain a fading downtrend. As selling pressure runs out, price breaks above the upper line. Stop below the wedge, target equal to the wedge's widest height.

Continuation Patterns A pause before the trend resumes
Continuation · Bullish

7. Falling Wedge

Inside an uptrend, price pulls back into a tightening, downward-sloping wedge. It's a corrective pause rather than a reversal — a break above the upper line resumes the original uptrend. Stop below the wedge, target its full height.

Continuation · Bullish

8. Bullish Rectangle

Price consolidates sideways between parallel support and resistance during an uptrend. A close above resistance confirms the trend is continuing. Entry on the breakout, stop back inside the range, target equal to the rectangle's height.

Continuation · Bullish

9. Bullish Pennant

A sharp rally (the flagpole) is followed by a small symmetrical triangle as the market catches its breath. A breakout above the pennant continues the move. Stop below the pattern, target measured from the flagpole's length.

Continuation · Bearish

10. Rising Wedge

Inside a downtrend, price stages a corrective bounce that tightens into a rising wedge. A break below the lower line resumes the downtrend. Stop above the wedge, target equal to its widest height.

Continuation · Bearish

11. Bearish Rectangle

Price consolidates between horizontal support and resistance during a downtrend. A close below support confirms sellers remain in control. Entry on the breakdown, stop back inside the range, target equal to the rectangle's height.

Continuation · Bearish

12. Bearish Pennant

A sharp sell-off is followed by a small symmetrical triangle as the market pauses. A break below the pennant resumes the downtrend. Stop above the pattern, target measured from the length of the initial move.

Bilateral Patterns Can break in either direction
Bilateral · Either

13. Ascending Triangle

A flat resistance line caps price while a rising trendline of higher lows squeezes from below. It usually resolves upward, but plan both sides: a break above resistance targets the triangle's height, while a break below the rising support flips the trade bearish.

Bilateral · Either

14. Descending Triangle

A flat support line holds price up while a falling trendline of lower highs presses from above. It usually resolves downward, but keep both scenarios ready: a break below support targets the triangle's height, a break above the falling resistance flips it bullish.

Bilateral · Either

15. Symmetrical Triangle

Two converging trendlines — falling highs and rising lows — squeeze price toward the apex with no clear directional bias. Wait for the confirmed break: enter in the direction of the close, stop on the opposite side of the triangle, target equal to its widest height.

DISCIPLINE

No strategy survives without risk control

These three rules sit underneath every strategy above — skip them and the edge disappears.

01

Position sizing

Risk a small, fixed percentage of the account on any single trade — commonly 1–2% — so that a losing streak never threatens the account itself.

02

Stop-loss placement

A stop is set at the point where the original trade idea is proven wrong, not at an arbitrary distance — usually just beyond the structure being traded.

03

Reward-to-risk ratio

Favour setups offering at least 1.5 to 2 times the amount risked, so that a trader can be wrong more often than right and still stay profitable.
